title: NumPy File Input and Output
goal: Persist arrays with save/load, read text and CSV data, and pack several arrays into one NPZ file.

topics.title: save and load
topics.body: np.save writes the array's bytes and dtype to a .npy file and np.load reads them back exactly; the file is binary, so text editors show noise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.save('/tmp/a.npy', np.arange(3))
print(np.load('/tmp/a.npy'))

topics.title: Text and CSV round-trip
topics.body: savetxt writes human-readable numbers and loadtxt parses them back as floats, which is the portable option when another tool must read the file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savetxt('/tmp/a.txt', np.array([1, 2]))
print(np.loadtxt('/tmp/a.txt'))

topics.title: Several arrays in one NPZ
topics.body: savez stores named arrays in a single compressed-free archive and load returns a mapping whose keys are the names you gave.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savez('/tmp/a.npz', x=np.arange(2))
print(list(np.load('/tmp/a.npz').keys()))

title: Advanced Data Types and Special Arrays
goal: Use structured dtypes, datetime64 and vectorised string operations for real records.

topics.title: Structured arrays
topics.body: A structured dtype names each field and its type, so one array can hold an id and a score and you can select a column with a['field'].
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f4')])
print(a['score'])

topics.title: datetime64 arithmetic
topics.body: A datetime64 array with a unit such as [D] supports addition of whole days, so date maths stays integer arithmetic underneath.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.array(['2026-01-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
print(d + 1)

topics.title: Vectorised string operations
topics.body: np.char applies string methods elementwise; it is convenient for arrays of text but it is not a replacement for proper text tooling.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['num', 'py'])
print(np.char.upper(a))

debug.title: A field the dtype never declared
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4')])
print(a['score'])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f4')])
print(a['score'])
debug.error: ValueError: no field of name score

debug.title: An impossible calendar date
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(['2026-13-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]'))
debug.fix:

title: Masked Arrays and Numerical Robustness
goal: Detect and handle NaN and infinity honestly, and choose masked arrays or nan-aware functions deliberately.

topics.title: NaN is not equal to anything
topics.body: isnan locates missing values and nanmean ignores them; plain mean propagates NaN, so one missing reading can hide the whole summary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.isnan(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: Infinity is a value, not a missing one
topics.body: isinf finds overflow and division-by-zero results; infinity is a real float value, so it must be filtered or clipped rather than treated as missing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf(np.array([1.0, np.inf])))

topics.title: Masked arrays carry their own mask
topics.body: A masked array stores a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions ignore masked positions — cleaner than overwriting values with NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.masked_array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 0])
print(a.mean())

debug.title: NaN silently wins the mean
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a.mean())
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.nanmean(a))
debug.error: prints nan — mean() propagates NaN; use nanmean when values are missing

debug.title: NaN cannot become an integer
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, np.nan], dtype=int)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, np.nan], dtype=float)
print(np.isnan(a))
debug.error: ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to integer

title: Performance and Vectorization
goal: Replace Python loops with vectorised code, reuse buffers with out= and benchmark changes honestly.

topics.title: Vectorised reduction
topics.body: One NumPy expression runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, so a million-element sum needs no Python iteration.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(1_000_000)
print(int((a * 2).sum()))

topics.title: Reuse a buffer with out=
topics.body: Passing out= writes the result into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in hot loops where the shape is already known.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out)

topics.title: Chunk large work
topics.body: array_split lets you process a big array in bounded pieces, which keeps peak memory predictable on datasets that do not fit comfortably.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(int(chunk.sum()) for chunk in np.array_split(a, 2)))

debug.title: An out array of the wrong shape
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(2)
np.add([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], out=out)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(3)
np.add([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], out=out)
print(out)
debug.error: ValueError: output array is not acceptable (shape mismatch)

debug.title: In-place add on an alias
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a
b += 1
print(a)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a.copy()
b += 1
print(a)
debug.error: prints [1 2 3 4 5] — b was the same object, not a copy

title: NumPy Ecosystem and Real-World Applications
goal: Move arrays between NumPy, Pandas, plots and model inputs, and know which layer owns which job.

topics.title: Pandas is built on arrays
topics.body: Series.to_numpy() exposes the underlying values, which is how you hand a column to a NumPy routine and keep the data, not the labels.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2])
print(s.to_numpy(), s.to_numpy().mean())

topics.title: Feature matrices are 2-D arrays
topics.body: A model expects one row per sample and one column per feature; reducing along axis 0 gives one value per feature, which is the shape a scaler fits.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(axis=0).shape)

topics.title: Images are (height, width, channels)
topics.body: An RGB image is a 3-D uint8 array and its shape is the first thing to check before any filter or model input.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.zeros((2, 2, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(img.shape, img.dtype)

debug.title: shape is an attribute, not a method
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.shape(0))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.shape[0])

debug.title: to_numpy takes no shape argument
debug.broken:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2])
print(s.to_numpy(shape=3))
debug.fix:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2])
print(s.to_numpy().reshape(2, 1))
